title: Travel writing

paragraphs.text: Travel accounts representing the observations and experiences of individuals who visited foreign lands long ago are an important primary source for historians. Such travel accounts can be valuable in several ways. They often provide details about foreign cultures that the actual inhabitants of those countries were unable to record, either because they did not have a way of doing so, or because they did not recognize these facts as particularly distinctive or interesting. Besides this, particularly talented or reflective travelers have sometimes been able to offer unusual insights which help historians understand the societies visited. But travel accounts are not just windows onto foreign societies, but also mirrors in which the authors reflect the values of their own cultures while recording their observations and experiences in faraway lands.

Records of foreign travel appeared soon after the invention of writing, but it was only with the formation of large imperial states in the classical world that travel accounts emerged as a prominent literary genre, appealing especially to rulers desiring useful knowledge about their lands. In researching the events that led to the Persian Wars, the Greek historian Herodotus reported on his travels in Egypt and Anatolia. The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian, writing about his travels while in search of allies for the Han emperors, described much of Central Asia as far west as what is now Afghanistan. Hellenistic and Roman geographers such as Ptolemy and Pliny the Elder relied on their own travels throughout the Mediterranean world, as well as on the reports of other travelers, to compile vast compendia of geographical knowledge.

During the post-classical era (about 500 to 1500 C.E.), two new purposes emerged as major incentives for travel to foreign lands. First, Muslim merchants sought trading opportunities throughout much of the Eastern Hemisphere. They described lands, peoples, and commercial products of the Indian Ocean basin from East Africa to Indonesia, and they supplied the first written accounts of societies in West Africa. While merchants set out in search of trade, every devout Muslim aimed to travel once in his lifetime on a pilgrimage to the Holy City of Mecca and thousands of them related their experiences. Between the 5th and 9th centuries C.E., Chinese Buddhists such as Xuanzang and Yijing traveled to India to study with Buddhist teachers and visit holy sites, recording their experiences as they traveled, and at the same time, Chinese merchants frequently visited Southeast Asia and India.

By no means did Muslim and Chinese travel come to a halt in the early modern era (about 1500 to 1800 C.E.). But as European peoples became familiar with the larger world of the Eastern Hemisphere — and the profitable commercial opportunities that it offered — they came to play a more dominant role in travel and travel writing, finding new routes to Asian and African markets, and setting up colonies in these areas. Their efforts eventually took them to the Americas and Oceania as well, and European printing presses churned out thousands of travel accounts that described foreign lands and peoples for a reading public at home with an apparently insatiable appetite for news about the larger world.

During the 19th century the focus was on exploration, as European travelers made their way from the coasts of Africa and the Americas to the interior, generating a fresh round of travel writing as they did so. By mid-century, attention was flowing also in the other direction. Asian travelers, such as the Japanese reformer Fukuzawa Yukichi and the Chinese revolutionary Sun Yat-sen, visited Europe and the United States to investigate different types of social organization.

With the development of inexpensive and reliable means of mass transport, the 20th century witnessed explosions both in the frequency of long-distance travel and in the volume of travel writing. As in ages past, a great deal of travel took place for reasons of business and administration, but new kinds of travel also flourished. The most distinctive of these was mass tourism, which emerged as a major form of consumption for individuals living in the world's wealthy societies. A peculiar variant of the travel account arose to meet the needs of these tourists: the guidebook, which offered advice on food, lodging, shopping, local customs, and all the sights that visitors should not miss seeing. Tourism has enabled consumers to get away to see the sights in Rome, take a cruise through the Caribbean, walk the Great Wall of China, or go on safari in Kenya, and it has had a massive economic impact throughout the world which still continues today.
